title: What is the Bain interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: Bain's hiring steps explained: application, first and second rounds of case and experience interviews, written cases in some offices, and preparation tips.
hook: For consulting roles, Bain's process usually runs from an application to an online assessment, then two rounds of interviews that each combine fit or experience questions with a candidate-led case, and in some offices a written case in the final round. Candidates often describe Bain's interviewers as friendly and supportive, but the bar is high. Here is how each stage works and how to prepare for it.
body:
In this guide

  • The steps
  • The online assessment
  • The case: candidate-led
  • The fit and experience questions
  • The written case

  • How to prepare
  • Common mistakes
  • Practice
  • Where to go next

The steps

Bain says its interviews are customised to the role, and that for consulting the process is a digital assessment followed by case interviews. Most generalist candidates see something like this, though details vary by office and year:

  1. Application: CV and cover letter screening, often through campus recruiting for students.
  2. Online assessment: a screening test before interviews.
  3. First round: usually two or more interviews of about 45 minutes with consultants and managers. Each typically opens with a fit or experience question or two, then a case of around 35 minutes.
  4. Final round: interviews with partners, in the same format, sometimes with a written case.
  5. Offer.

Confirm the exact format with your recruiter; it changes by office, role and year.

The online assessment

Bain describes its online assessment as a screening test you complete before interviews, and offers preparation resources through its digital assessment hub. Use those first, follow your invitation's instructions exactly, and keep your mental maths and data-reading sharp. Online tests and digital cases covers how to approach firm assessments in general.

The case: candidate-led

Bain cases are usually candidate-led. The interviewer gives you the prompt and expects you to clarify the objective, build a structure, decide where to start, ask for data, do the maths and land a recommendation. Interviewers generally step in only if you go badly off track, so you need to keep the case moving yourself. Ask for data before making assumptions, and say why each piece of analysis matters.

Bain's preparation pages emphasise structured, logical thinking and note that it provides all the materials you need. You do not need specialist industry knowledge. How to drive a case is the key skill to build.

The fit and experience questions

Expect questions about your background, your motivations and why Bain. Bain's careers site says it looks for intellectual curiosity, entrepreneurial drive and enthusiasm for challenges, and wants candidates to explain why they want to join Bain specifically. Some roles include conversations with future colleagues about your past experience and Bain's operating principles.

Partners in the final round often go deeper into your career story and what you want next. Prepare a clear narrative of where you have been and where you want to go, plus stories about teamwork, leading others and results.

Weak: "Bain has a great culture and I really like the people I've met."
Strong: "I want to work on problems where the result is measurable. The consultants I spoke to described projects where the team stayed until the client's numbers moved, and that is the kind of accountability I want early in my career."

The strong answer is specific, connects to real conversations and could not be pasted into an application for another firm. See why consulting, and why this firm.

The written case

Some Bain offices use a written case in the final round. You receive a pack of data or slides, work alone for a set time to build a short set of slides with your analysis and recommendation, then present and discuss them with an interviewer. What matters:

  • skim the whole pack first, then read only what answers the question;
  • work out the three or four numbers that decide the answer;
  • write action titles that state the insight;
  • leave time to rehearse a two-minute summary.

How to handle written cases goes into more detail.

A worked practice case

Run this as a 35-minute mock with a partner. (Illustrative numbers.)

Prompt: A gym chain is considering opening ten new locations. Should it?

First two minutes: clarify the decision and the success criteria. Say the client wants each site to pay back within seven years.

Structure: market demand in the target areas; site economics; the chain's capabilities to open ten sites at once; and alternatives, such as fewer sites or franchising.

Ask for data, then calculate. Each site costs $2M upfront and is expected to reach 2,000 members paying $40 a month, with $650k a year in running costs.

  • Revenue per site: 2,000 × $40 × 12 = $960k a year.
  • Operating profit per site: $960k − $650k = $310k a year, before financing, tax and depreciation.
  • Ten sites: $3.1M a year on $20M of investment.
  • Simple payback: $2M ÷ $310k ≈ 6.5 years, inside the seven-year target, but only just.
  • Break-even membership: $650k ÷ ($40 × 12) ≈ 1,354 members per site.

Push further. Payback assumes full membership from day one. If a site averages only 1,200 members in its first year, it loses 1,200 × $480 − $650k = −$74k that year, and payback slips beyond seven years. Membership churn, maintenance spending and cannibalisation of existing sites all need checking.

Recommend.

"I'd open the four sites with the strongest demand first rather than all ten. At full membership each pays back in about 6.5 years, just inside the target, but a slow first year pushes it over. Opening in waves lets us check real ramp-up before committing the remaining $12M."

Afterwards, have your partner score you separately on clarity of the objective, tailored structure, data requests, maths, synthesis and collaboration. Separate scores show you exactly where to improve.

How to prepare

  • Use Bain's case interview prep hub and digital assessment resources.
  • Practise candidate-led cases where you drive from structure to recommendation. Our casebook has full cases to run with a partner.
  • If your office uses written cases, practise reading a data pack quickly and building three or four clear slides against the clock.
  • Prepare stories about teamwork, leadership and results, and a specific answer to why Bain.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting for the interviewer. In a candidate-led case, say what you want to look at next and why.
  • Assuming instead of asking. Ask for data first; make assumptions only when it is not available.
  • Stopping at the average. "Payback is 6.5 years" is not a recommendation. Say what it means against the target and what could change it.
  • Generic motivation. "Great culture" is not an answer to why Bain.

Practice

1. The client raises the price to $45 a month and expects membership to fall to 1,800. What happens to operating profit per site?

Show the answer

Revenue: 1,800 × $45 × 12 = $972k. Profit: $972k − $650k = $322k, up from $310k. The price rise more than offsets the lost members. Payback improves slightly to $2M ÷ $322k ≈ 6.2 years.

2. Give a one-sentence answer to "Where would you start?" in the gym case.

Show the answer

"I'd start with the economics of a single site, because if one site cannot pay back within seven years, the question of ten is answered." It shows prioritisation and links the analysis to the decision.

Where to go next

Compare with McKinsey's process, read payback and NPV to sharpen investment cases like the gym example, and continue with the Deloitte process.
